title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We report a preregistered paired trial (N = 500 intents) that measured whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) gate—one shared LLM generation per intent, deterministic verification, and up to one automated repair—reduces verifier‑unsafe accepted network changes relative to accepting the LLM candidate (LLM‑only baseline) on a standardized synthetic NetOps workload. The preregistered execution used gpt-5-mini as the declared generator under shared_initial_generation semantics and a deterministic network verifier that enforces canonical parsing, sequencing/workflow policies, group/availability constraints, paired‑field dependencies, and final‑state equality to the intended expected_final_state. Observed accepted final changes: baseline 496/500 (0.992), guarded (GVR) 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The preregistered exact conditional two‑sided McNemar test on the discordant margin (n = 4, k = 4) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we therefore do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. A predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for four initial candidates (one repair attempt each); total hosted model calls observed = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls), mean model calls per accepted change = 504/500 = 1.008. We reconcile the McNemar and bootstrap perspectives, document verifier semantics and known blind spots, clarify provider‑call accounting semantics, present representative repaired‑episode diagnostics, and point readers to the archived evidence bundle and preregistration for full machine‑readable artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation from human intent to device configuration promises reduced toil for network operators but also risks: incorrect or mis‑ordered CLI sequences can violate workflow, dependency or availability constraints and cause outages. Recent work explores LLMs for intent translation and broader AIOps tasks, but hallucination and factual errors remain primary reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation is to gate LLM outputs with deterministic verification and, where possible, apply bounded automated repairs. This study asks whether a compact GVR pipeline—single shared LLM generation per intent, deterministic verification, and at most one automated repair—reduces verifier‑unsafe accepted changes relative to accepting the LLM candidate (LLM‑only baseline) on a standardized synthetic workload.

We executed a fully preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) on N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles (50 intents per profile). The run used gpt-5-mini as the declared generator under a shared_initial_generation contract (one initial model call per intent reused by both conditions), a deterministic network verifier implementing a compact rule set matched to the synthetic intent grammar, and a GVR controller that issued at most one repair prompt per failing candidate. All seeds, task generation, and analysis were frozen and archived prior to execution. All numerical quantities reported here are taken verbatim from the archived execution and analysis artifacts.
sections.related_work: Our experiment intersects three literature strands. First, surveys and systems work document active adoption efforts for LLMs in NetOps and AIOps and repeatedly highlight hallucination and factual errors as deployment obstacles; these motivate adding deterministic validation gates to tool‑augmented agentic pipelines [doi:10.1002/nem.2313; https://openalex.org/W4411735779; https://openalex.org/W4415071524; https://openalex.org/W4406137434]. Second, methodological proposals for evaluate‑and‑repair architectures recommend standardized validator semantics, paired trial designs, frozen preregistration, and explicit accounting for orchestration costs (model calls, repair attempts); these blueprints shaped our preregistered paired estimator, shared_initial_generation semantics, and provider accounting definitions [https://openalex.org/W4403443637]. Third, deterministic configuration verifiers and scalable analysis tools can check syntax, sequencing/workflow patterns, availability constraints, and dependency rules at scale; such verifiers detect many classes of LLM mistakes but vary in control‑plane fidelity and vendor coverage [https://openalex.org/W4413757123]. Our study situates a compact, evidence‑grounded GVR gate within this prior work: we evaluate a single‑model GVR pipeline over a controlled synthetic benchmark to measure verifier‑detectable safety improvements and orchestration cost under a strict preregistered contract rather than to claim immediate production readiness across vendor heterogeneity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The full design was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. The primary estimand is the paired per‑intent success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) across 500 paired intents. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on discordant pairs; a predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) was retained for descriptive estimation.

Execution contract and orchestration semantics: The execution contract fixed generation semantics: for each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared model (gpt-5-mini) and that same candidate was used by both the baseline (accept shared candidate) and guarded (validate shared candidate, repair if failing) conditions. Retrieval‑augmented generation was disallowed and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1. Provider accounting is recorded as hosted model call events; the archived provider audit reports model_calls_used = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4) and stage_counts showing shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 4. Under the preregistered contract repaired pairs therefore exhibit two model calls (shared initial + one repair); the mean model calls per accepted change equals 504/500 = 1.008.

Deterministic verifier and scoring: The adjudicating verifier canonicalizes CLI sequences and deterministically checks a predeclared rule set tuned to the synthetic intent grammar. Checks include: (i) syntactic parsing and normalization; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome; valid = true indicates verifier PASS. For each episode the verifier emits a normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, a violation list and codes, and valid. The verifier intentionally omits vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing/convergence simulation, session/execution‑time errors, and hardware resource constraints; therefore verifier PASS is necessary for experiment safety but not sufficient for production safety.

Repair policy and prompt semantics: When the verifier fails the shared_initial candidate the GVR controller constructs a constrained repair prompt containing the original intent abstraction, the verifier violation codes with short descriptions, and explicit instruction to produce a corrected canonical CLI sequence. At most one automated repair attempt was permitted per failing episode; the repair candidate was accepted only if the verifier returned valid = true. All repair prompts/responses and verifier traces for repaired episodes are archived and are the basis for the repaired‑episode diagnostics reported below.

Statistical analysis: The preregistered confirmatory test conditions on the observed discordant margin and evaluates a two‑sided binomial tail on k = n10 with p = 0.5 (exact conditional McNemar). The predeclared exploratory paired bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) was computed on paired binary outcomes without conditioning on the observed discordant margin. Analysis executors, seeds, and result files were frozen and archived prior to manuscript drafting.
sections.results:
Execution completeness and primary counts: The run completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 1000; complete_pair_count = 500) with no failed episodes. Observed accepted‑change counts: baseline 496/500 (0.992); guarded 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked in four episodes; each repair attempt produced a subsequent verifier PASS. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 504 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair = 4).

Preregistered inferential outcomes: The preregistered confirmatory test conditions on the discordant margin n = n10 + n01 = 4 and evaluates the two‑sided exact conditional McNemar on k = n10 = 4. The one‑sided tail P(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16; doubling for two‑sided yields p = 0.125. Under the preregistered decision rule this p‑value does not meet the confirmatory threshold (per‑test alpha = 0.025 after the preregistered multiplicity plan) and we therefore do not claim confirmatory significance.

Exploratory paired estimate: The predeclared paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.002, 0.016], with point estimate 0.008. This exploratory interval was predeclared and computed without conditioning on the observed discordant margin; with only four discordants the percentile interval can exclude zero because resamples repeatedly include the small favorable discordant set. We present the bootstrap interval descriptively while adhering to the preregistered McNemar decision rule for the primary claim.

Repaired‑episode diagnostics: The four repaired/discordant pairs corresponded to verifier‑detectable sequencing or group/paired‑field dependency violations. The archived verifier violation codes and short descriptions are:
- pair-000090 | [MUST_BE_DOWN_FOR_FIELD] — VLAN/field changed while interface remained admin up; required 'must be down' sequencing violated. Repair invoked; final_score: PASS.
- pair-000341 | [MAKE_BEFORE_BREAK] — Backup uplink not enabled before primary was shut; violates 'make‑before‑break' availability rule. Repair invoked; final_score: PASS.
- pair-000381 | [PAIRED_MTU_CHANGE] — MTU changed on one side of a paired link without coordinating the paired interface's MTU change. Repair invoked; final_score: PASS.
- pair-000413 | [GROUP_AVAILABILITY_CONSTRAINT] — Both edge interfaces placed admin down simultaneously, violating minimum_active_in_groups availability constraint. Repair invoked; final_score: PASS.
Representative per‑episode validator traces, repair prompts/responses, and normalized configurations are archived in the evidence bundle. Numerical totals and contingency counts above are taken directly from the archived analysis artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Reconciling inferential perspectives: Numerically the GVR pipeline intercepted four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that the baseline would have accepted; these four correspond to the observed discordants (n = 4, k = 4) and yield a raw paired increase of 0.008. The preregistered exact conditional McNemar conditions on the observed discordant margin and computes an exact two‑sided binomial tail; with n = 4 this yields p = 0.125, conservative for small discordant counts and not meeting the preregistered confirmatory threshold. The predeclared exploratory bootstrap percentile CI excludes zero ([0.002, 0.016]) because bootstrap resampling does not condition on margins and can repeatedly sample the few favorable discordants. Both perspectives are informative: the McNemar enforces the preregistered confirmatory decision rule and guards against overstating evidence when discordants are rare; the bootstrap interval provides a descriptive magnitude estimate but with weaker frequentist coverage guarantees under very small discordant counts. We therefore report both results but adhere to the preregistered McNemar for our primary claim.

Operational interpretation: Under the bounded repair policy (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) the repair invocation rate was 4/500 (0.8%), generating modest extra model calls (hosted model call events = 504). In this synthetic workload the compact deterministic verifier acted as a low‑latency gate that removed verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals with minimal orchestration cost. In practice realized benefit and cost tradeoffs depend on baseline failure rates, verifier runtime at inventory scale, adversarial or more diverse intent distributions, and latency/throughput requirements for higher‑fidelity verifiers.

Verifier scope, sufficiency, and blind spots: The verifier enforces canonical normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency rules, and final‑state equality to expected_final_state. These checks detected the four repaired episodes in this run. Critically, the verifier omits vendor‑specific CLI semantics, control‑plane timing and convergence modeling, session execution errors, and hardware resource constraints; therefore verifier PASS is necessary but not sufficient to guarantee production safety. Production automation would require expanded verifier fidelity (vendor parsers, control‑plane simulators, timing/convergence models) and telemetry‑driven validation (pre‑ and post‑change) before unsupervised execution.

Threats to validity and generality: Strengths include preregistration, frozen seeds, deterministic task generation, complete execution accounting (complete_pair_count = 500; failed_episode_count = 0), and archived traces for audit. Key limitations: (1) Construct validity is constrained by the verifier abstraction and synthetic device templates—rules match the synthetic intent grammar but imperfectly model vendor control‑plane hazards. (2) External validity is limited by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies; multi‑model replication and vendor‑specific parsing are required to generalize. (3) Confirmatory sensitivity was reduced because the preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 but the observed baseline was near ceiling (496/500 = 0.992), producing only four discordants and limited realized power. These explain why a modest numerical paired difference appears in the exploratory bootstrap interval but not under the preregistered exact McNemar decision rule.

Practical implications and engineering tradeoffs: For organizations adopting LLM‑driven intent translation, a compact deterministic verifier used as an automated gate plus a bounded repair loop can intercept many verifier‑detectable unsafe proposals with low model‑call overhead in workloads similar to our synthetic setting. Engineering decisions—verifier fidelity, permitted repair depth, model selection, and latency budget—must be calibrated against operational risk tolerances, expected baseline error rates, and adversarial threat models. Finally, the preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this run; therefore the planned multiplicity adjustment for two confirmatory tests was not applied to the present confirmatory test.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 produces an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016] while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; therefore we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance under the preregistered decision rule. Deterministic verification combined with a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in the studied synthetic setting; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated‑automation comparator which was not executed in this run. Archival artifacts including the preregistration, model configuration, raw results, per‑episode verifier traces, provider accounting, and analysis logs are available in the evidence bundle for independent verification and audit (see the preregistration record).

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an explicit autonomy lock. The generation model used in the archived run was gpt-5-mini (declared_model_version recorded in the archived model configuration). Key automated components in the run were a deterministic task generator, a deterministic network verifier, and a GVR controller implementing shared_initial_generation plus at most one automated repair per task. The study was preregistered under study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here are: N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The immutable initial master prompt for this run is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt) and its SHA‑256 is 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. The design, preregistration, code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and this revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed in this archived run; therefore the original preregistered multiplicity plan that would have adjusted for two confirmatory tests was not applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to the deterministic verifier’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation across two planned tests is not applicable to the present execution.
